newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka to build power plant despite protests.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka to build power plant despite protests.

text.p: Sri Lanka's state power utility said on Tuesday it will go ahead with a planned coal-fired power plant on the northwest coast despite protests by residents of the area.
"We're going ahead with the project," a senior Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) official said. "There is no other site...no other option."
The CEB has said it plans to construct a 300 megawatt coal-fired power plant in Kalpitiya, in the Puttalam district, about 160 km (100 miles) north of the capital Colombo.
One man was killed and several others injured when police fired on residents demonstrating against the planned power plant last week.
Residents have said they oppose the project because of fears of environmental pollution and loss of land.
But CEB officials said the plant is urgently required to meet rising power consumption and cut dependence on hydro-electric power, which in recent years has been badly affected by drought.
The CEB recently banned the use of air-conditioners and urged private sector businesses to use their own generators.
The restrictions were imposed after water levels in reservoirs, which supply 85 percent of grid power, plunged to dangerously low levels because of low rainfall.

But CEB officials said last Friday that the utility was unlikely to impose more limits on use of grid power as water levels in depleted reservoirs have held steady with the onset of intermonsoon showers.
However, they said electricity tariffs might have to be raised to meet the costs of a sharp rise in diesel consumption to fuel power plants.
Newspapers have reported that the government is considering a 30 percent increase in tariffs.

The CEB has said it plans to cut dependence on hydro-electricity to 57 percent of the requirement by building more thermal power plants by June 1997. The island now has an installed capacity of 1,135 megawatts of hydro-electric power and 250 megawatts of thermal power.
